en: The Sūtra on the Analysis of Dependent Origination,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of Western Heaven, the Imperially Enfeoffed Grand Officer, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master for the Transmission of the Teaching, Dharma Deva, in obedience to the Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying by the side of Lake Uruvilvā, near the Nairañjanā River, beneath the Bodhi tree. Not long after his enlightenment, he dwelt there alone, and this thought arose in his mind:
"The phenomena of suffering in the world cannot be avoided and cannot be feared; they exist with certainty and reality. To observe them in this way is of great significance and benefit."
The worldly delight in dharmas is likewise thus: none can escape it, none can grow weary of it, yet it exists with certainty and reality; to observe it in this way brings great benefit.
He further reflected:
"Within all the realms of the world—whether among devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—none are able to fully comprehend this Dharma."

If there is another person who is well able to contemplate, who remains alert to suffering and pleasure, and who thus thoroughly understands that these are not ultimate dharmas—constantly reflecting upon this and practicing in accordance with the Dharma—this person shall attain the dharmas of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation in their entirety.

All Buddhas of the past and future have fully awakened to and known the suffering and pleasure of the world; they have understood each and every thing and practiced according to the Dharma, attaining perfect enlightenment through the power of their own practice.

Why is this? This Dharma has never existed before, and there is no one capable of fully comprehending it. All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past fully understood each aspect of this Dharma, practiced according to the Dharma, and thereby attained perfect enlightenment.

In future ages, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will likewise fully comprehend all such worldly phenomena as suffering and pleasure, and by practicing in accordance with the Dharma, they shall realize the fruit of the perfect path.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, by the Buddha’s majestic power, knew the Buddha’s thoughts; then, like a strong man bending and extending his arm, he departed from the Brahma realm and came to where the Buddha was.
Having completed his prostrations, he stood before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Just as the Buddha has contemplated, so it is: among the sufferings and pleasures of the world, there is none who can escape them; this is of great significance and benefit, and it is likewise for the past and the future."

Within the realms of devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, understands each and every thing—whether increasing or decreasing, whether good or evil—and can distinguish them all; he understands the phenomena of dependent origination as they truly are through the power of his Buddha-wisdom.
The Buddha said: "Brahmā King! It is so, it is so."

Sentient beings in the world lack wisdom and discernment regarding all phenomena; unable to comprehend them, they are shrouded and obstructed by the darkness of ignorance and delusion—this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; these volitional formations are of three kinds, namely: bodily, vocal, and mental.

Furthermore, conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; this consciousness is of six kinds, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise.
"Name" excludes form; it consists of four types, namely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and all derivative material phenomena, which are produced from the four great elements.
Thus, these two aggregates—the aggregate of form and the aggregate of name—are what constitute name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

From the condition of name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise. As for the internal six sense bases, there are six kinds, namely: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
Conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; there are six kinds of contact, namely: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
Furthermore, conditioned by contact, feeling arises; there are three kinds of feeling, namely: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by feeling, craving arises; there are three kinds of craving, namely: craving for sense-desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless.

Furthermore, conditioned by craving, grasping arises; there are four kinds of grasping, namely: grasping at sense-pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, and grasping at the doctrine of self.

Furthermore, conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*) arises. Existence is of three kinds: namely, existence in the realm of desire (*kāma-bhava*), existence in the realm of form (*rūpa-bhava*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpya-bhava*).

Conditioned by existence, the phenomenon of birth (*jāti-dharma*) arises. As for this phenomenon of birth, it refers to the realm of sentient beings; it arises in accordance with the aggregates (*skandha*), distinguished in every instance, being a phenomenon that is born and perishes differently, constantly shifting and changing.

Taking birth as the basis, there are the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*), as well as phenomena such as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); these are called "birth.

With birth as a condition, there are aging and death. What is called "aging" refers to the clouding of consciousness, white hair, wrinkled faces, diminished physical strength, moaning and labored breathing, a frail body, and the complete decay of all the faculties (*indriya*); this is called "aging.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of "death"?

"Death" refers to the fact that all distinctions among the realms and destinies of sentient beings ultimately revert to impermanence; when the limit of their lifespan is exhausted, they relinquish warmth, the life-faculty ceases, the aggregates are abandoned, and the four great elements disperse—this is called death.
As previously stated, aging and death constitute these two factors.
"What has been thus described is called the analysis of the dharma of dependent origination."
"If any sentient beings are able to understand this, such persons shall attain the fulfillment of the fivefold Dharma-body.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the dharma of dependent origination, the Brahma King prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew, returning to the realm of Brahmā.
The Sūtra on the Analysis of Dependent Origination Spoken by the Buddha
